Brent's Method in One Dimension

Source: R/brent.R
brent.Rd

Minimizes a function of one variable without derivatives: a bracket of the minimum is found by golden expansion from the starting value, and the bracket is then reduced by Brent's combination of parabolic interpolation and golden-section steps.

Usage

brent(
  criterion = crit_stationary(1e-05),
  step = 1,
  max_expand = 50,
  maxit = 100,
  max_eval = Inf,
  verbose = FALSE,
  refresh = 1,
  keep_trace = FALSE
)

Arguments

criterion

The stopping rule, a criterion() object. Defaults to crit_stationary(1e-5), which reads the half-width of the bracket, so the tolerance is on the scale of the parameter, or on the unconstrained scale when lower or upper is given. A rule that needs a gradient is rejected when the run starts.

step

The length of the first trial step of the bracketing phase, a single positive number, default 1.

max_expand

How many golden expansions the bracketing phase may take, a single number of at least 1, default 50. If the phase has not bracketed a minimum by then, the run stops at the lowest point evaluated and reports converged = FALSE.

maxit

Maximum iterations of the reduction phase. Defaults to 100.

max_eval

Maximum objective evaluations. Defaults to Inf.

verbose

Report progress? Defaults to FALSE.

refresh

Report every this many iterations. Defaults to 1.

keep_trace

Store the iteration path? Defaults to FALSE.

Value

An S7 object of class Brent, inheriting from optimizer(), to be handed to minimize().

Details

The bracketing phase evaluates the starting value \(x_0\) and \(x_0 + h\), turns round if the second is the higher, and steps on in the descending direction, where each step is \(1.618\) times the previous one, until the value no longer falls. The three points then satisfy \(f(b) \le f(a)\) and \(f(b) \le f(c)\) with \(b\) between \(a\) and \(c\), so a minimum lies in \([a, c]\). If the value is still falling when max_expand expansions have been taken, or when the evaluation budget runs out, the phase has not bracketed a minimum, and the run stops at the lowest point evaluated, reports converged = FALSE and records the reason in message.

The reduction phase is the algorithm of Brent (1973, chapter 5). At each iteration the parabola through the three best points is tried first; its vertex is accepted when it lies inside the bracket and the step is less than half the step before last, and a golden-section step into the larger part of the bracket is taken otherwise. Parabolic steps converge superlinearly on a smooth minimum, and the golden steps bound the number of evaluations when the function is not well modeled by a parabola. The stationarity measure is the half-width of the bracket.

The rule receives iter, f_new, f_old, x_new, x_old and stationarity; f_old and x_old are those of the previous iteration and are NULL at the first. Besides the rule, the reduction stops on Brent's own test, when the bracket has shrunk to about \(\sqrt{\varepsilon}\,\lvert x \rvert + 10^{-12}\) around the best point \(x\), because at that width a further point cannot be distinguished from \(x\). That stop reports converged = TRUE with criterion_met equal to bracket at machine resolution, so a rule with a smaller tolerance than this resolution, or crit_never(), ends there.

The method is for one parameter only; a starting value of any other length is rejected. Bounds are removed by the same reparametrization as in the other methods (see bounded_transform()).

References

Brent, R. P. (1973). Algorithms for Minimization without Derivatives. Prentice-Hall, Englewood Cliffs.

See also

nelder_mead() for the derivative-free method in several dimensions, crit_stationary() for the default rule of this method.

Examples

brent()
#> <optimizer> brent
#>   stop when : stationarity < 1e-05
#>   budgets   : maxit 100, evaluations Inf
#>   settings  : step = 1, max_expand = 50

# The method minimizes a smooth function of one variable.
f <- function(x) (x - 2)^2 + exp(-x)
r <- minimize(brent(), f, par = 0)
c(par = r@par, evaluations = r@counts[["f"]])
#>         par evaluations 
#>    2.063504   12.000000 

# nelder_mead() is run on the same function for comparison.
minimize(nelder_mead(), f, par = 0)@counts[["f"]]
#> [1] 42
